questions.prompt: What does mensural/proportional rhythmic notation primarily communicate, according to Andreyev?
choices: A Exact clock-time durations in milliseconds for every note.
B Proportions between durations, not an absolute duration by itself.
C Only dance steps with no relation to note values.
D Exclusive use of unequal Balkan beats with no Western equivalents.
questions.explain: The system represents proportional durations between values, not an absolute duration alone.

questions.prompt: In 4/4 time, what does the time signature tell you?
choices: A The beat unit is a half note with three per bar.
B The basic beat unit is the quarter note, with four quarter notes per bar/measure.
C There are eight whole notes per bar.
D Meter is undefined until the final double bar.
questions.explain: 4/4 means quarter-note beat unit and four quarters per bar (measure).

questions.prompt: Which statement best matches Andreyev’s account of beat strength in a 4/4 bar?
choices: A All four beats are equally strong.
B Beat 1 (downbeat) is strongest; 2 weak; 3 stronger than 2 but weaker than 1; 4 weakest.
C Beat 4 is always the strongest accent.
D Only beat 2 receives an accent.
questions.explain: He graphs 4/4 with strongest downbeat, weak 2, medium-strong 3, weakest 4.

questions.prompt: How does he distinguish 3/4 from 6/8 in terms of grouping/beaming?
choices: A 3/4 is two groups of three; 6/8 is three groups of two.
B 6/8 beams as two groups of three; 3/4 beams as three groups of two.
C They are identical in pulse grouping.
D 6/8 uses only whole notes; 3/4 uses only thirty-seconds.
questions.explain: 6/8 pulses in two groups of three; 3/4 in three groups of two—visible in beaming.

questions.prompt: What are asymmetric meters such as 5/4 or 7/4, in his taxonomy?
choices: A Meters that combine duple and triple groupings into one meter; common in folk traditions, rare in early Classical/Baroque.
B Only possible in electronic DAWs.
C Forbidden after the invention of the bar line.
D Identical to compound ternary 9/8.
questions.explain: Asymmetric meters (5/4, 7/4, etc.) combine groupings; common in folk music, uncommon in Classical/Baroque until later.
